title: Who can say no
question: How often does a project that meets the rules still get pulled into a hearing, how long does that add, and who asks?
finding: Since 2015 members of the public filed 887 requests for discretionary review, a hearing on a project that otherwise meets the code. Each took a median 135 days to close; the Planning Commission changed the project in 27%, left it unchanged in 23%, and 33% were withdrawn. Projects that drew one took a median 525 days at Planning against 352 for other projects needing a hearing or review. The City's published records name the person who asked on 4 of the 887, so whether a few people file many cannot be checked.
how: Planning Department records of type DRP (public-initiated discretionary review) opened since 2015, with their closing status; project days run from the project record opening to closing. The other rows count the separate approvals a project can need on top of its building permit.
limits: Asking for review is a legal right, usually used by neighbours, and some requests end in a negotiated change that both sides accept. The published records leave the requester's name blank, so repeat filers cannot be counted from them; the hearing packets name each requester. The data does not record payments made to settle a request; that is the abuse the rule is said to invite, and only a hearing record or a court file could show it.
